title: Terminal survival kit: what the shell does to your line
objectives: Predict what the shell hands a program after quoting and expansion: `'…'` vs `"…"`, `~`, `$VAR`, globs, and zsh's `no matches found`
Spot the zsh-vs-bash traps — an unquoted `$VAR` isn't split, `path` is tied to `PATH` — and write the quoted or array form that works in both
Route output with `>`, `>>`, `2>&1` and `|`, and explain why `> file 2>&1` and `2>&1 > file` differ
Chain commands on exit codes with `&&`, `||` and `pipefail`, and predict when `a && b || c` runs `c`
Explain how `PATH` and `export` decide what a command and its children see, and why a script or a tool's shell can't see your terminal's setup

sources.title: GNU Bash manual: Lists of Commands
Apple Support: Use zsh as the default shell on your Mac

questions.prompt: `cd "~/Documents"` fails with `cd: no such file or directory: ~/Documents`, but `cd ~/Documents` works. Why?

options.text: The shell expands `~` only when it's unquoted, so `cd` received a literal `~/Documents`
`cd` doesn't understand `~`; only commands like `ls` do
Double quotes switch off every expansion, exactly like single quotes
The folder doesn't exist; the quotes are irrelevant

questions.explanation: `cd` doesn't expand `~` itself — the **shell** does, before the command runs, and only for an unquoted `~` at the start of a word. Double quotes are *not* the same as single quotes: inside `"…"`, `$VAR` and `$(…)` still expand, which is why `cd "$HOME/Documents"` works and is the right way to quote a path with spaces.

questions.prompt: In zsh, `open https://example.com/search?q=git` prints `zsh: no matches found: https://example.com/search?q=git` and nothing opens. What happened?

options.text: `?` is a glob character; no file matched the pattern, and zsh refuses to run a command whose glob matches nothing
`open` can't parse URLs that contain a query string
zsh blocks unquoted URLs as a security measure
The page returned no results, and `open` reported it

questions.explanation: `?` matches any one character in a file name, so the shell tried to expand the URL as a filename pattern — before `open` ever ran. zsh's default (`NOMATCH`) is to stop with an error when nothing matches; bash would have passed the text through unchanged. Quote anything containing `?`, `*` or `[`: `open 'https://example.com/search?q=git'`.

questions.prompt: In zsh: `FILES="old.log debug.log"` then `rm $FILES`. What happens?

options.text: `rm` receives one argument, `old.log debug.log`, and fails: no such file
Both files are removed
Only `old.log` is removed
zsh stops with `no matches found`

questions.explanation: zsh doesn't split an unquoted parameter on spaces (the `SH_WORD_SPLIT` option is off), so `$FILES` stays one word. Bash *would* split it and remove both — which is why bash snippets misbehave when pasted into zsh. Hold a list in an array: `files=(old.log debug.log); rm "${files[@]}"` works in both shells. `no matches found` is a glob error; there's no glob here.

questions.prompt: A zsh script runs `for path in src/*.ts; do wc -l $path; done` and then `pnpm lint`. Every pass of the loop prints `command not found: wc`, and `pnpm lint` fails with `command not found: pnpm`. Why?

options.text: zsh ties the array `path` to `PATH`; each pass replaced the command search path with a file name
`for` loops run in a subshell that drops `PATH`
The glob consumed the arguments meant for `pnpm`
`pnpm` is never available inside scripts

questions.explanation: In zsh, `path` (lowercase) is an array tied to `PATH`: assign one and the other changes. The loop variable is assigned before the body runs, so even the first `wc` is looked up in a `PATH` that is just the first file name; after the loop, `PATH` is the last file name, and no command can be found. A subshell would have *protected* your `PATH`, not dropped it. In bash, `path` is an ordinary variable and the same loop is harmless. Name loop variables `file`, `f` or `dir`. A `local path=…` inside a zsh function clobbers `PATH` for the rest of that function too.

questions.prompt: You want everything `pnpm build` prints — normal output **and** errors — in `build.log`. Which line does that?

options.text: `pnpm build > build.log 2>&1`
`pnpm build 2>&1 > build.log`
`pnpm build | tee build.log`
`pnpm build 2> build.log`

questions.explanation: Redirections apply left to right, and `2>&1` copies where stdout points *at that moment*. In `> build.log 2>&1`, stdout already points at the file, so stderr follows it there. In `2>&1 > build.log`, stderr is pointed at the terminal first and stdout moves afterwards, so errors still hit the screen. A pipe carries only stdout, so `| tee` misses the errors unless you write `2>&1 | tee build.log`. `2>` alone captures only the errors.

questions.prompt: A CI step runs `pnpm test | tee test.log`. Three tests fail, yet the step is green. Why, and what fixes it?

options.text: A pipeline's exit code is its last command's — `tee` succeeded. `set -o pipefail` makes a failing stage fail the pipeline
`tee` hides stderr from CI; redirect errors with `2>&1` to fix it
CI ignores the exit code of any piped command by design
`pnpm test` exits 0 whenever its output isn't a terminal

questions.explanation: Everything downstream judges a step by its exit code, and a pipeline reports the **rightmost** command's status unless `pipefail` is set (bash and zsh both have it; then the last non-zero status wins). `tee` copied the text fine, so the pipeline exited 0. Adding `2>&1` would put the error text in the log, but the exit code would still be `tee`'s.

questions.prompt: `setup.sh` contains `cd app` and `export NODE_ENV=production`. You run `./setup.sh` from `~/shop`. Afterwards, in your terminal:

options.text: You're still in `~/shop` and `NODE_ENV` is unchanged — the script ran in a child process with its own copies
You're in `~/shop/app` and `NODE_ENV` is `production`
You're still in `~/shop`, but `NODE_ENV` is `production` — `export` sends it back up
You're in `~/shop/app`, but `NODE_ENV` is unset

questions.explanation: Running a script starts a new shell process. It gets a *copy* of your environment and its own working directory; `cd` and `export` change those copies, and they vanish when it exits. `export` only reaches processes started *after* it, from that shell — children, never the parent. To run the commands in your current shell, `source ./setup.sh`.

questions.prompt: `pnpm` works in your terminal. A git pre-commit hook fails with `pnpm: command not found` — but only when you commit from a GUI git app opened from the Dock. Your `export PATH=…` line is in `~/.zshrc`. Why?

options.text: The hook's shell descends from the app, not your terminal; nothing in that chain was an interactive zsh, so `.zshrc` never ran and its PATH addition is missing
Git hooks always run in bash, and bash can't read `PATH`
Hooks run in a sandbox that blocks package managers
`pnpm` refuses to run while git holds the index lock

questions.explanation: zsh reads `.zshrc` only for **interactive** shells. A commit started from your terminal inherits the terminal's exported `PATH`, so the hook works there. An app launched from the Dock never went through your terminal, so it has only the system's default `PATH`. Git runs the hook with whatever interpreter its first line names — often `#!/bin/sh`, which reads none of your zsh files (a zsh hook would read only `.zshenv`). Bash itself reads `PATH` fine; the value is what's missing. The fix that works for every caller: set `PATH` at the top of the hook, or call tools by absolute path.

prompts.prompt: Send both stdout and stderr of the build into one file.
prompts.explanation: `2>&1` makes stream 2 (stderr) point wherever stream 1 (stdout) points now — and because it comes after `> build.log`, that's the file. zsh and bash both also accept `&> build.log` as shorthand for the whole thing.

prompts.prompt: Loop over a list of file names — one of them has a space — in a way that works in both zsh and bash.
prompts.explanation: `"${files[@]}"` expands to every element, each as its own word, spaces intact — in both shells. A space-separated string (`FILES="a.txt my notes.txt"`) can't do this: zsh keeps it as one word, and bash splits `my notes.txt` into two.

prompts.prompt: Make `API_URL` visible to the dev server you start next from this shell.
prompts.explanation: A plain assignment creates a shell variable that only this shell can read. `export` puts it in the environment that every program started afterwards receives a copy of. For a one-off, `API_URL=http://localhost:4000 pnpm dev` sets it for that single command.

prompts.prompt: Print the message only when `grep` finds no match (it exits 1 then).
prompts.explanation: `||` runs the right side when the left side exits non-zero. `grep` exits 0 on a match, 1 on no match and 2 on an error (such as a missing file) — so this also prints the message when `notes.txt` doesn't exist, which may or may not be what you want.

prompts.prompt: In `~/.zprofile`, put `~/.local/bin` first in the command search path without losing the rest.
prompts.explanation: `PATH` is searched left to right and the first match wins, so prepending makes your directory take priority. Forget `:$PATH` and you replace the whole list — the next `ls` fails with `command not found`.

code: for f in $FILES; do echo "[$f]"; done
snippets.question: What does zsh print?
acceptable: a single iteration with the whole string
snippets.explanation: One iteration: zsh doesn't split an unquoted parameter, so `$FILES` is one word. The same two lines in bash print `[a.txt]` and `[b.txt]`. If you need the split in zsh, say so with `${=FILES}` — or better, store a list in an array to begin with.

snippets.question: What appears in the terminal?
snippets.answer: Two lines: ls: nope: No such file or directory — then a.txt
acceptable: the error line, then a.txt (from cat)
the error on screen; only a.txt in the file
snippets.explanation: Left to right: `2>&1` points stderr at the terminal (where stdout points *now*), then `> out.txt` moves only stdout. So the error goes to the screen, and the file holds just `a.txt`, which `cat` prints. Swap the order — `> out.txt 2>&1` — and both lines land in the file. (The error text shown is macOS `ls`; GNU `ls` words it slightly differently.)

snippets.question: What do the three lines print?
snippets.explanation: `&&` and `||` have equal precedence and group left to right. Line 1: `false` skips A, so the list failed and `|| echo B` runs. Line 2: `true && false` failed — at the *second* step — so C runs anyway; that's why `a && b || c` isn't if/else. Line 3: `true || echo D` succeeds without running D, so `&& echo E` runs. Same output in zsh and bash.

snippets.question: What do the last two command lines print?
acceptable: unchanged and empty after zsh; app and dev after source
snippets.explanation: `zsh goto-app.sh` runs the file in a **child** shell: it changes directory and exports `STAGE` in its own process, then exits, leaving yours untouched. `source` runs the same lines in **your** shell, so the `cd` and the `export` stick. That's why you `source ~/.zshrc` after editing it rather than executing it.
